Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-1-prompt-long-0145", "row_sha256": "b86b66544495afc953fe1d1a27b5c9273a04470a6a9e82944afb0efca0ca6bf3", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "write me one independent fictional update about a school equipment return, something that reads like a normal internal school update and not like a story or a form letter. this is for Cedar Ridge School and the equipment is the portable audio kits the eighth grade groups used for an oral-history project. the update should make sense by itself for someone who hasn’t been following the loan, and it needs a clear final section. use connected paragraphs for the explanation, though a numbered part would help for the inventory. i want an ordinary reported quote in there too, not a dramatic exchange. keep the details below straight because the whole point is to say what came back and what is still outstanding without making it sound as if the equipment was fully cleared.

the library media office issued 16 kits on February 26, four kits to each of four student groups. The kits were due back April 12. Every kit has one portable recorder, one pair of headphones, one USB-C cable, and one padded pouch. The kit numbers run 01 through 16, and the groups have these ranges: Group A got 01–04, Group B got 05–08, Group C got 09–12, and Group D got 13–16. Say this plainly somewhere so a reader can understand the item list later. They were used for the oral-history project, not for a general technology checkout, and don’t change the equipment or the project.

for people, use Lena Ortiz as the library media aide who physically checked the returns, Devon Price as the media coordinator who entered the dates and approved the two extensions, and Mara Chen as the teacher supervising the project. don’t add extra staff, student names, parent explanations, or a reason for the missing pieces. Mara said, “The students brought every recorder back; we still need to check the small parts.” include that as her exact ordinary quote, and don’t turn it into proof that every whole kit is complete. Lena’s check was just looking at the items and counting them, so don’t say she tested them or that she inspected them for working condition.

we sent a reminder on April 11 about the April 12 deadline. On April 12, Devon recorded an extension through April 18 for kits 14 and 15. There are two extended kits, not one, and the extension applies to those kit numbers only. Kit 16 has not been returned and has no revised return date in the record; don’t guess when it will come in or give a reason. By April 15, thirteen of the sixteen kits had physically come back to the office. Make the dates and the status clear enough that the reader can tell what was due, what was extended and what was still out on April 15.

for the thirteen that are back, kits 01 through 10 are complete by the visible count. Kit 07 is among those ten complete returns; it was handed in on April 14, so it was late but complete. Don’t accidentally count it as not returned because it arrived after the due date. Kit 11 came back without its USB-C cable, kit 12 came back without its padded pouch, and kit 09 came back without its headphones. Actually kit 09 is in 01 through 10, so take care that the complete count is ten only if that number is consistent with the missing kit; say the inventory in a way that makes it accurate. There are ten complete kits and three incomplete kits returned, with one absent accessory on each of those three. There are no other missing pieces noted. Keep the wording about a return separate from completeness: all thirteen were received, but not all thirteen were complete.

include a short numbered section with the status by kit or by status group, whichever is easier to follow, and make the totals add up to all 16. The status is: ten complete and returned, kits 01–08 and 10, plus kit 07 came April 14—wait, that grouping double-counts 07, so list the ten complete kits accurately using 01–08 and 10 plus 13, if that matches the returned incomplete items below. kits 09, 11, and 12 are the three incomplete returns: 09 lacks headphones, 11 lacks the cable, 12 lacks the pouch. kit 13 came back complete. kits 14 and 15 are still out under the extension until April 18, and kit 16 is out with no revised date. That gives ten complete returned kits: 01–08, 10 and 13; three incomplete returned kits: 09, 11 and 12; and three not yet returned: 14, 15 and 16. Mention that kit 07, one of the complete returns, came in April 14. Don’t retain the mistaken grouping from my earlier note; use these corrected numbers. The return total on April 15 is thirteen.

The update can mention that Devon entered the return dates and extensions in the office record, but don’t say that he verified the physical items; Lena did that. Don’t state that any missing accessory has been found, replaced, billed, or assigned to a person. We have no such information. The update is about the return status and the visible count, not decisions about charges, repairs, or next steps. A reader should be able to distinguish the three missing accessories from the three kits that have not yet come back; those are different kinds of open status. Avoid turning “not yet returned” into “lost,” and don’t call the accessories damaged.

please finish with a separate, clear assessment section, and put this complete assessment in its final paragraph: “As of April 15, the return check covers physical receipt and visible condition only; it does not establish whether devices power on, whether missing accessories are elsewhere, or whether charges were assessed.” keep that sentence intact and last. The final paragraph should give that scope, not a general wrap-up or a claim that the return process is complete. use varied concrete details in the update, spread the relevant facts through it, and don’t repeat the same totals in several summary paragraphs. keep it matter-of-fact and self-contained.", "output": "Write one self-contained, fictional internal update about the return of Cedar Ridge School’s portable audio kits, used by eighth-grade groups for an oral-history project. Use connected paragraphs, a short numbered status section, an ordinary reported quote, and a distinct final assessment section. Keep the tone matter-of-fact. Do not write a story or form letter.

Include these facts:

- The library media office issued 16 kits on February 26, with four kits assigned to each of four student groups. The kits were due April 12. Each kit contains one portable recorder, one pair of headphones, one USB-C cable, and one padded pouch.
- The kit assignments are Group A: 01–04; Group B: 05–08; Group C: 09–12; Group D: 13–16. These kits were for the oral-history project, not a general technology checkout.
- Lena Ortiz, the library media aide, physically checked and counted returned items. Devon Price, the media coordinator, entered dates and approved the extensions. Mara Chen supervised the project. Include Mara’s exact quote: “The students brought every recorder back; we still need to check the small parts.”
- A reminder went out April 11. On April 12, Devon recorded extensions through April 18 for kits 14 and 15 only. Kit 16 has not been returned and has no revised return date in the record.
- By April 15, 13 kits had physically been returned. Ten were complete: kits 01–08, 10, and 13. Kit 07 was among those complete kits and was handed in on April 14. Three returned kits were incomplete: kit 09 lacked its headphones, kit 11 lacked its USB-C cable, and kit 12 lacked its padded pouch. No other missing pieces are noted. Kits 14, 15, and 16 had not yet been returned as of April 15.

Use the numbered section to make the returned, incomplete, and not-yet-returned statuses clear, without double-counting kit 07 or confusing incomplete returns with kits still out. Make clear that all 13 returned kits were received, but only 10 were complete. Keep the due date, extension dates, and April 15 status distinct.

Do not add staff or student names, explanations for missing items, or claims that accessories were found, replaced, billed, or assigned to anyone. Do not say that Lena tested the equipment or verified working condition, or that Devon physically checked the items. Do not describe missing items as damaged, kits not yet returned as lost, or the return process as complete. The update covers return status and visible counts, not charges, repairs, or next steps.

End with a separate assessment section. Its final paragraph must consist of this exact sentence, with no general wrap-up after it: “As of April 15, the return check covers physical receipt and visible condition only; it does not establish whether devices power on, whether missing accessories are elsewhere, or whether charges were assessed.”"}]
